newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM to visit Okinawa to address US base woes.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM to visit Okinawa to address US base woes.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Tuesday will travel to Okinawa in an effort to mend ties with the restive southern island where resentment against a heavy concentration of U.S. military bases runs high.

Hashimoto's visit with a high-powered team of economic ministers aims to underscore the central government's commitment to easing the burden of the concentration of U.S. bases and promoting economic development.

The prime minister will travel to Okinawa with one eye on the election calendar and the other on the United States, which is anxious to avoid damage to Japan-U.S. security ties, seen by both sides as vital to regional security.

Japanese Defence Minister Hideo Usui and Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda on Thursday meet their U.S. counterparts in Washington for broad discussions on bilateral military cooperation in the region surrounding Japan.
After the one-day Okinawa trip, Hashimoto is expected to huddle with top officials from his three-party ruling coalition and set a date for a general election.
Polls, though not mandated until July 1997, are expected to be held as early as October 20.

The thorniest political problem faced by Hashimoto's government eased last week when Okinawa's governor agreed to take steps to renew the leases for the U.S. military bases on the island, ending a bitter one-year standoff with Tokyo.
The leases, held by some 3,000 landowners opposed to the bases, expire next May, posing a potential threat to U.S. use of the facilities and complicating Japan-U.S. security ties.
Okinawa Governor Masahide Ota took a hardline stance on the bases after three U.S. servicemen raped a local schoolgirl last year, sparking anti-base protests on the island.

The populist governor relented after Hashimoto pledged to shrink the bases and set up a five-billion-yen ($45.8-million) fund for the economic development of Okinawa prefecture, the poorest in Japan with average income half the level of Tokyo's.
Hashimoto last week warned Japan against complacency on Okinawa, telling reporters, "We are, of course, far from a solution to the Okinawa problem."

The subtropical island, about 1,000 km (625 miles) southwest of Tokyo, is home to three-quarters of the U.S. military facilities and about half of the 47,000 U.S. military personnel stationed in Japan, although it constitutes less than one percent of the country's total land area.
In a referendum on September 8, Okinawans voted overwhelmingly for shrinking the U.S. military presence, resented for noise, accidents and crime by U.S. troops.

The vote was seen as registering Okinawan dissatisfaction with President Bill Clinton's announcement during his visit to Japan in April of base consolidations that reduce the area they occupy by about 20 percent.

The ink was no sooner dry on the Hashimoto-Ota pact last week when Okinawa police said two U.S. servicemen were being held by U.S. authorities on suspicion of assaulting and robbing a female bar owner.
Okinawans have long complained about the heavy concentration of U.S. bases on the island.

Devastated in World War Two as the only major Japanese island to experience ground battles, strategically placed Okinawa was under U.S. rule for 27 years until 1972, during which time U.S. authorities appropriated land for military bases.
